Individual semistructured interviews were conducted with 12 relatives of male farmers who had died by suicide in Queensland or New South Wales, Australia (2006-2014).

Queensland (QLD) farmer suicide cases were identified utilizing the Queensland Suicide Register (QSR), a suicide mortality database managed by the Australian Institute for Suicide Research and Prevention (AISRAP).
Individual semistructured interviews were conducted with 12 relatives of male farmers who had died by suicide in Queensland or New South Wales, Australia (2006-2014).

Twelve male farmers (including 1 farm manager) (Mage = 60.17, SD = 7.17), who died by suicide, were each represented by an informant, a close next-of kin (NOK) who had lived with or known the deceased well.

Individual semistructured interviews were conducted with 12 relatives of male farmers who had died by suicide in Queensland or New South Wales, Australia (2006-2014).

The current investigation was conducted in accordance with the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative research (COREQ) checklist.17 This project was approved by the Griffith University Human Research Ethics Committee (CSR/08/13/HREC).
Upon receipt of this form, the clinical interviewer (LK) contacted the informant to arrange an interview (conducted September-December 2015).
[/page/1/Text/13] Semistructured telephone interviews were conducted in a confidential room with 12 individuals who had lost a close NOK male farmer to suicide.

This study employed a generic (inductive) qualitative approach with a focus on human experiences.24 Twelve participants were included in the analysis. The purposive sampling provided a homogenous group of the size considered optimal to the generic qualitative approach.17 The 5 steps for conducting thematic analysis as by Braun and Clark25 were followed: familiarizing with the data (each individual transcript was read and reread highlighting ideas for codes/themes); initial codes were generated and organized into meaningful groups; different codes were sorted into potential themes and collated to establish relationships between codes, themes and different subgroups of themes; themes were reviewed to ensure distinctions between themes were clear; and themes were defined and named to determine clearly what aspect of the data was captured by each theme. Initial procedures were carried out by the first author (LK).
The present study extends understanding of suicide among Australian male farmers using a qualitative approach to analyze PA interviews with close relatives.

PA studies are subject to recall bias as data are based on retrospective report of informants following a suicide, potentially providing a skewed understanding of a loved one's cognitive process and behaviors prior to death.18 Second, only one informant could be interviewed per deceased farmer; hence, our data reflect the perception of those family members interviewed.

Six interrelated themes were identified: (1) masculinity, (2) uncertainty and lack of control in farming, (3) feelings of failure in relationships and farming, (4) escalating health problems, (5) maladaptive coping, and (6) acquired capability with access to means.

Six interrelated themes with major overlaps were identified: (1) masculinity, (2) uncertainty and lack of control in farming, (3) feelings of failure in relationships and farming, (4) escalating health problems, (5) maladaptive coping, and (6) access to means with acquired capability for suicide.

Wearing a mask was reportedly an important aspect of adhering to masculine norms of socialization. Most men were described as conscientious with a quiet or shy personality. They had a propensity to hide or suppress emotions; however, in order to socialize they would wear a mask or a cutout cardboard version as a coping strategy. Attitudes and beliefs of a rural masculinity, such as self-reliance, stoicism and a strong work ethic, and describing farmers as battlers and heroes are strongly embedded within the sociocultural norms of the occupation. For farm owners, there was a sense that farmers possessed a strong sense of self-worth in the role of a provider and attached importance to being a good farmer. X was a quiet man . . . a battler. . . always such a hard worker all his life . . . and didn't like to have other people do things for him . . . . Anger went inward instead of coming out . . . he was a very private person, and he couldn't cope with not being able to work . . . . If he wasn't on a tractor making hay or doing something with the cattle, he was out with a hoe in his hand. He loved his farm . . . . Farming and his family was number one in his life. Anything else just hopped in line behind that . . . . (F3)

evidence.section_title: (2) Uncertainty and Lack of Control in Farming: "Money and nothing in your control"
evidence.quote: Prolonged drought was experienced by all of the farmers and reflected the uncertainty and lack of control over farming. As drought ensued, expenses increased (eg, buying water); consequently, workload increased, incidents of physical illness/injury increased, and financial security was threatened. As a consequence of drought and subsequent financial problems, a number of factors contributed to elevating distress among the farmers, including: change to family roles (spouses gaining employment and hence becoming absent from daily home routine and social interaction); feelings of uncertainty and incompetence around farm foreclosure, age, and not having skills to start other employment; loss of animals (selling or death of animals held in family for generations); increased costs (water, hay, transport); and increased farm expenditure (eg, cost of repairing machinery, threat of plant disease, regulation changes, and increased bank interest rates).

evidence.section_title: (3) Feelings of Failure in Relationships and Farming: "I don't like looking in the mirror"
evidence.quote: [page/3/Text/9] Farmers felt that they were failing in their relationships and it seemed to be an important proximal factor contributing to suicide. This was interrelated with cultural norms of masculinity and with the family, land and the commodity. Norms associated with subsequent feelings of failure included: family-of-origin expectation of the farm staying in the family name (succession farming); sons inheriting the family farm; keeping up with other farmers in the district (eg, having enough stock during drought); land autonomy; and antiauthoritarian attitudes to regulatory procedures.

evidence.section_title: (i) Mental health problems "I'm in a dark place"
evidence.quote: Difficulty in communicating (eg, minimizing symptoms and needs) in response to a number of interrelated stressors involving loss of personal control, rejection and failure to achieve expected work or family goals was commonly reported. Externalizing (eg, irritability, anger, aggression, alcohol abuse, or increasing workload), somatic (eg, hypersomnia or insomnia, fatigue), painful somatic/physical conditions (back pain, tinnitus, and headaches) were more commonly reported than internalizing (eg, ruminating, withdrawal, anxiety, and depression) symptoms. He said one day, "I don't like looking in the mirror." I said, "What do you see?" He said, "I see someone very angry," but he also saw a failure . . . . He did look very angry. He'd say he was going to work, but he'd go and sleep . . . . He wouldn't have many drinks to be really drunk. He had just given up. (F6) Negative cognitive processes were reflected within the narratives (ie, guilt, shame and regret, anger with frustration, jealousy, pessimism, paranoia, and cognitive distortion or rigidity). Internalizing disorders such as depression and anxiety (eg, isolation, withdrawal, rumination, and negative bias), externalized coping (ie, verbal/physical aggression, increased alcohol/cannabis consumption ("self-medicating"), low engagement in health care (ie, priority of work over health, lack of mental health knowledge, minimization of pain and severity/seriousness of illness, and low treatment adherence); and suicidality (despair, hopelessness, worthlessness, and perceived burdensomeness) were also reported. A small number of farmers experienced long-term mental health disorders since early adulthood, with frequent hospitalization, suicide exposure and communication of intent to health professionals reported. He'd always been very active . . . never rested, because he used to have this idea – he used to say, "I've got to work like crazy while I can, to make up for the times when I won't be able to do anything." . . . That used to drive him and he'd have that fear that – how long would it last? He might be well for 2 weeks, and then 2 weeks later he'd be lying in bed 24/7 and wouldn't get up. (F6)

evidence.section_title: (ii) Physical health "Not a person to give in"
evidence.quote: Most farmers reported protracted concerns about physical health before their death but continued to work. In addition to experiencing injury from farm-related incidents (ie, spinal injury and industrial auditory injury), they experienced gastroenterology disorders (eg, gastroesophageal reflux disease) and chronic pain (eg, osteoarthritis). Farmers were fearful of the future with regard to increasing health concerns and pharmacological treatment as health declined, inability to work, and experienced increasing pain, fatigue, and sleep difficulties; however, they were stoic in their resolve to continue farming.

Stress was managed by employing unconscious avoidance strategies, such as increasing time working, increasing consumption of alcohol or cannabis, or engaging in aggressive behaviors directed at their romantic partner, parents, animals, or objects.This pain at night, he couldn't sleep, he was getting worse . . . right through 2013, '14, he was buying sherry and he was hiding it up in the shed. I think in the end that was the reason that he maybe – he came down that day when the tractor had jacked him up again, and he had completely lost it up there . . . . (F10)Problem solving and decision-making became increasingly more difficult for most farmers with interpersonal conflict and relationship breakdown becoming salient acute stressors prior to death. Farmers largely coped with relationship stress and breakup alone (eg, did not seek legal or financial advice, did not seek help from relatives or friends), engaged in impulsive behaviors (eg, sold stock, machinery), and increased consumption of alcohol and cannabis.

evidence.section_title: (6) Acquired Capability with Access to Means: "People who live on farms know how to kill things"
evidence.quote: The relationship with firearms and farming was commonly reported. There was an assumption that a firearm is the most likely suicide method because most farmers possess a firearm "and know how to kill things." Although not necessarily used on a regular basis, firearms were considered an occupational tool—"it's there if it is needed." An informant stated that "firearms were X's only possession." Another informant stated that the events leading to the farmer's death were indicative of the farmer's awareness of diminished physical capacity for the occupation, access to lethal means, and the functional role of a firearm. One farmer's gun license had been revoked due to a psychiatric diagnosis. Another had experienced the death of a child to suicide by firearm and subsequently, relinquished firearms during the national gun-buy-back scheme.
